channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Alongside tighter regulation, firms pushed voluntary green moves: battery maker CATL certified all 20 of its plants carbon-neutral in core operations and set a 2035 value-chain target, and Neste and Toray built a renewable-nylon supply chain.
item.description:
While Europe's rulebook tightens by force, parts of the industry are moving on decarbonisation by choice. CATL, the world's largest battery maker, said it achieved its 2025 goal of carbon neutrality across core operations, with all 20 of its plants certified, and laid out a roadmap to a carbon-neutral full value chain by 2035 — a benchmark from a heavy manufacturer many suppliers sell into. In specialty materials, Neste, Goldwin, Idemitsu Kosan and Toray established a supply chain to make nylon fibre from renewable raw materials rather than fossil feedstock, with the fibre already used in sportswear. Brazil's Senate separately passed a "Profert" law offering tax incentives to build domestic fertilizer production and cut import reliance — another sign of governments and firms reshaping chemical value chains around sustainability and security.

Industry Impact

Bio-based and low-carbon feedstocks are becoming a competitive differentiator as customers and regulators demand lower product carbon footprints. For Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) makers, credible renewable-content and carbon-neutral offerings increasingly unlock premium segments and large-customer supplier scorecards, while laggards face both regulatory cost and lost tenders. CATL's value-chain target is a concrete signal that major buyers will push emissions requirements upstream to their chemical suppliers.

Associated Press | Cefic | Associated Press

item.title: Southeast Asia kept beating expectations: Thailand grew 1.9% year-on-year in the second quarter, Singapore's non-oil exports rose 19.4% on an electronics and AI upcycle, and Vietnam moved to build a domestic materials industry.
item.description:
Regional data surprised on the upside. Thailand's economy expanded 1.9% year-on-year in the second quarter, slightly above expectations and better than earlier fears that growth would roughly halve. Singapore's non-oil domestic exports grew 19.4% in the first seven months and 24.2% year-on-year in July, powered by electronics — where exports jumped 112% — riding the global artificial-intelligence investment wave. Vietnam, meanwhile, set out to develop its own materials industry to strengthen strategic autonomy and master core technologies, aiming to reduce dependence on imported inputs. The common thread is a region benefiting from supply-chain diversification away from China and from booming demand for AI-related electronics, even as some domestic sectors stay soft.

Industry Impact

Southeast Asia is an expanding manufacturing base for electronics and assembly, lifting demand for electronics adhesives, encapsulants and coatings, and it is an increasingly important production location as companies diversify supply chains. Vietnam's materials-industry ambition signals more local competition upstream over time but also more local demand for specialty chemicals near new plants. The region deserves a growing share of commercial attention relative to a cooling Chinese consumer market.

Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener | Vietnam News

item.title: Global carmakers are doubling down on China: GM–SAIC extended their joint venture to 2047, with Volkswagen and Honda renewing too, even as Chinese vehicle exports jumped 72.5% and Chinese brands reached nearly 20% of UK registrations.
item.description:
Despite losing ground to domestic rivals at home, foreign automakers are committing to China for the long term. General Motors and SAIC extended their venture by 20 years to 2047, and Volkswagen–SAIC and Honda–GAC signed renewals — a bet that access to China's supply chains, engineering talent and scale outweighs the pain of shrinking local market share. The competitive backdrop is China's export surge: passenger-car exports rose 72.5% to about 5.4 million units in January–July, and July vehicle exports climbed 81.3% to 1.043 million, with new-energy vehicles up 145.5% and now 60% of the mix. The reach is visible in Europe, where Chinese-owned brands already account for 19.59% of 2026 UK vehicle registrations, and in Latin America, where Chinese models top some sales charts.

Industry Impact

The automotive sector is a major end-market for structural adhesives, sealants and coatings, and its centre of gravity is shifting toward Chinese OEMs and Chinese-built electric vehicles. Suppliers whose relationships are anchored to legacy Western brands risk under-indexing on the fastest-growing customers; deepening ties with Chinese automakers and their European plants is increasingly where volume growth sits. The JV renewals also keep foreign OEMs — and their qualified supplier lists — active in China through the next decade.

Xhby.net | Caixin Global | The Nation | ECG Association

item.title: EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc will propose its most far-reaching Russia sanctions this autumn, as Russia's budget deficit widened to RUB 5.45 trillion in the first half and its top court barred the Yabloko party.
item.description:
Kaja Kallas told German media the EU plans to significantly expand its Russia sanctions in the coming months, calling it the bloc's most far-reaching package yet, aimed at further cutting the revenue funding the Ukraine war. Enforcement of existing measures is already biting the periphery: crypto exchange Binance said it will stop processing transactions for 16 platforms and service providers, including HTX, to comply with EU sanctions. Russia's public finances are under strain — the consolidated budget deficit widened to about RUB 5.45 trillion in the first half of 2026 as oil-and-gas revenue fell. Politically, the Supreme Court upheld the exclusion of the liberal, anti-war Yabloko party from the September Duma elections and rejected its appeal, tightening the Kremlin's grip ahead of the vote.

Industry Impact

Each sanctions round widens compliance obligations for chemical and industrial exporters — more restricted entities, tighter dual-use and payment screening, and rising secondary-sanctions risk for firms dealing with intermediaries. Companies with any residual Russia-linked exposure, including through third countries, should expect the autumn package to add names and categories, and keep counterparty screening current rather than reactive.

South China Morning Post | The Moscow Times | Interfax | Handelsblatt

item.title: Eurostat confirmed the euro area grew 0.4% quarter-on-quarter in the second quarter despite the Iran war, with Spain a leading driver, while UK unemployment slipped to 4.9% but consumer sentiment and house prices softened.
item.description:
Final data confirmed eurozone GDP rose 0.4% in the second quarter, holding up better than feared given the drag from the Iran war and higher energy costs. Spain, the currency area's fourth-largest economy, was among the main engines of growth. The UK picture was more mixed: the unemployment rate fell to 4.9% in the three months to June, down from 5.0%, but the S&P Global consumer-sentiment index dipped to 42.9 in August from a four-month high, and asking prices for newly listed homes saw their steepest August fall in years. Together the readings suggest European economies are grinding out modest growth rather than accelerating, with resilient labour markets offset by cautious consumers and a cooling housing market.

Industry Impact

Modest but positive European growth supports a stable — not booming — baseline for construction, automotive and industrial demand, the end-markets for most adhesives, sealants and coatings. Spain's outperformance and firm labour markets are mild positives, but soft consumer confidence and falling house prices in the UK caution against expecting a strong second-half rebound in building and renovation activity. Planning around low-single-digit volume growth remains the prudent base case for Western Europe.

Handelsblatt | The Independent | The Independent

item.title: The US dollar fell to a two-month low after weak data, including an unexpected drop in retail sales, led traders to scale back bets on a near-term Federal Reserve rate rise, leaving the rate outlook finely balanced.
item.description:
Soft US economic readings, most notably an unexpected fall in retail sales, prompted markets to walk back expectations that the Federal Reserve would raise rates soon. The dollar dropped to a two-month low against the euro and held near multi-month lows against most major currencies. The signals were mixed rather than uniformly weak: the New York Fed's manufacturing index rose to 20.6 in August, its highest in four years, on stronger new orders, while average US petrol prices sat about 30% higher than a year earlier — a squeeze on households traceable in part to the Iran war's effect on oil. The net effect is a market leaning back toward the view that the Fed will stay on hold, reversing the brief mid-month scare that a hike was coming.

Industry Impact

A weaker dollar makes US exports more competitive but raises the local-currency cost of dollar-priced inputs — including crude, naphtha and many petrochemicals — for buyers outside the US. For European producers, a softer dollar and firmer euro can pressure transatlantic price competitiveness. The mixed data leave the rate outlook finely balanced, so treasury and procurement teams should keep hedges flexible rather than commit to a single Fed path.

The Economic Times | Channel News Asia | MarketScreener | Anadolu Agency

item.title: China's robotics push accelerated: the World Robot Conference opened in Beijing, Unitree lists in Shanghai on 19 August after a CNY 6.1 billion share sale, and national AI-computing capacity jumped 177% year-on-year.
item.description:
Beijing hosts the annual World Robot Conference this week, showcasing an ecosystem the city has built out, including a dedicated "Robot Mall". The event coincides with a wave of fundraising: Unitree, which makes humanoid and quadruped robots, begins trading in Shanghai on 19 August after raising CNY 6.1 billion, while Tsinghua-backed Robotera plans to raise up to USD 1 billion in Hong Kong to fund dexterous hands and humanoids. Underpinning it all, China's "intelligent computing" capacity — the specialised data-centre power used to train and run AI — reached 2,185 EFLOPS by end-June, up 177% year-on-year. Provincial hubs from Hunan to Mianyang are reporting 27–30% annual growth in local robot-industry chains. The signal: China is turning a research push into an industrial-scale, well-capitalised robotics and AI supply base.

Industry Impact

A scaling robotics industry expands demand for the engineering adhesives, thermal-interface materials, potting compounds and specialty coatings that go into robots, sensors and data-centre hardware — a growth pocket for industrial-chemicals suppliers. It also intensifies competition in factory automation itself, where cheaper Chinese robots could lower the cost of automating chemical and manufacturing plants. Suppliers positioned in electronics and assembly materials stand to benefit; those slow to serve the segment risk ceding it to local players.

Asharq Al-Awsat | The Standard | People's Daily | Bjd.com.cn

item.title: War in Iran and drought-hit waterways drove shipping rates on four key global routes to record highs at once: Persian Gulf-to-Asia oil freight reached USD 15.22 a barrel, the most since tracking began in 2005.
item.description:
Price-assessment agency Argus reported that freight rates on four major waterways rose simultaneously, an unusual convergence. The cost of shipping oil from the Persian Gulf to Asia hit USD 15.22 a barrel on 10 August, a record since the route was first tracked in 2005, as the Strait of Hormuz blockade forced longer, riskier voyages and higher war-risk insurance. At the same time, long-running drought has cut water levels on rivers and canals in Europe and the Americas, limiting how much cargo ships can carry and squeezing capacity. The twin pressures — geopolitical on one side, climatic on the other — are lifting the baseline cost of moving goods and raw materials worldwide, on top of the earlier rise in container and tanker rates.

Industry Impact

Higher freight feeds straight into landed costs for chemical raw materials and finished goods, and hits companies that depend on Rhine and other inland-waterway shipping in Europe — a route already constrained by low water in recent alerts. Manufacturers should expect freight surcharges to persist while both the war and the drought continue, and revisit sourcing that assumes cheap, reliable long-haul and inland shipping.

Commercial Times | Yahoo Taiwan

item.title: New-home prices across China's 70 major cities fell 3.2% year-on-year in July, but monthly declines are narrowing; Beijing launched a five-year, CNY 15 trillion urban-renewal programme to shore up construction demand.
item.description:
Property remains the soft spot in China's economy. New-home prices were down 3.2% year-on-year in July, yet the month-on-month picture improved: prices rose or held steady in 23 cities, and first-tier existing-home prices edged up 0.2%, suggesting official support is slowly finding a floor. To reinforce it, the government launched a CNY 15 trillion urban-renewal programme covering roughly 500,000 dilapidated homes and 115,000 ageing communities over five years, raised the maximum housing-provident-fund loan, and Beijing became the first city to implement the new stabilisation policy after a July Politburo meeting. The scale signals Beijing wants renovation and upgrading — rather than new-build sprawl — to carry construction demand as the sector matures.

Industry Impact

Urban renewal is directly relevant to Henkel's construction beat: renovation of ageing housing stock drives demand for sealants, tile adhesives, waterproofing and insulation coatings, often more per square metre than new build. If the CNY 15 trillion plan is funded and executed, it partly offsets the drag from falling new-build starts and shifts the opportunity toward repair-and-upgrade product lines. The open question is delivery — past Chinese stimulus headlines have outrun the money that actually reached the ground.

Macrobusiness | China Economic Net | Lianhe Zaobao | Bjd.com.cn

item.title: China's July activity data disappointed: industrial output grew 4.5% year-on-year, down from 5.3% in June, and retail sales rose only 0.6% against forecasts near 1.5%, signalling weak domestic demand even as high-tech output and exports stayed robust.
item.description:
The National Bureau of Statistics reported that factory output slowed to 4.5% growth in July from 5.3% a month earlier, held back partly by extreme weather. Retail sales — the main read on household spending — grew just 0.6%, well short of the roughly 1.5% analysts expected and down from 1% in June. The soft patch sits alongside continued strength at the top end: value-added output in high-tech and equipment manufacturing rose about 16.9%, and mechanical and electrical products made up 63.8% of exports in January–July. Total goods trade rose 17.3% over the same period. The picture is a two-speed economy — an advanced-manufacturing and export engine running hot while consumers stay cautious, weighed down by a weak property market and job insecurity.

Industry Impact

Soft Chinese consumption caps demand for consumer-facing goods and the adhesives, coatings and packaging that go with them, while the high-tech build-out supports demand for electronics-grade and industrial specialty chemicals. For suppliers, this argues for tilting exposure toward China's advanced-manufacturing and export sectors rather than broad consumer demand, and for watching whether Beijing adds stimulus to lift household spending in the second half.

The Guardian | Channel News Asia | China Daily | Global Times

item.title: Fresh EU regulation is raising the compliance load on the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) chain: new rules on classifying hazardous substances now hit paints and coatings, and a rewritten Product Liability Directive widens exposure.
item.description:
Several regulatory threads converged. Under the EU's tightened CLP system — the law that governs how chemicals are classified, labelled and packaged for hazard — obligatory classification now applies to new substances and, from 1 May 2026, to new mixtures. For paint and coating makers this means reworking formulations, safety data sheets and labels. In parallel, the EU's rewritten Product Liability Directive broadens who can be held liable for a defective product and extends the rules to software and AI-enabled goods, lowering the bar for claims against manufacturers. Finland's chemical-industry federation warned that a proposed widening of the national waste tax would add cost. And trade friction reached basic chemicals: Pakistan imposed a provisional 10.85% anti-dumping duty on soda ash from China — a feedstock for glass, detergents and industrial processes. Together these show Europe layering compliance duties onto formulators just as trade barriers spread in upstream chemicals.

Industry Impact

For Henkel and its peers, the direct effect is higher fixed cost per product: reclassification, relabelling and documentation absorb technical staff and slow new launches, while the wider liability regime raises the stakes on formulation records and substance data. Firms with strong regulatory-affairs capacity gain an edge over smaller competitors that struggle to keep up, and the soda-ash duty is a reminder that even commodity inputs now carry trade-policy risk worth designing around.

European Coatings | BRC | Kemianteollisuus | Business Recorder

item.title: New 50% US tariffs on about USD 20 billion of Canadian goods take effect on 19 August; Trump invoked a 1930s trade law after courts questioned his earlier tariffs, while negotiators discussed cutting car duties to 15%.
item.description:
The 50% duties on a wide range of Canadian exports are due to start on 19 August, and last-minute talks in Washington had not produced a deal. To underpin the new tariffs, the Trump administration invoked Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act — an almost-never-used clause allowing duties on countries deemed to discriminate against US commerce. The move follows court setbacks that threaten the emergency-powers basis of his earlier "reciprocal" tariffs, so the administration is now spreading its tariffs across several legal foundations to make them harder to strike down. Amid the pressure, negotiators explored a narrower bargain: cutting US duties on Canadian vehicles to 15% if a minimum share of each car's content is North American, in exchange for Canadian concessions on autos, metals and lumber. Trump also threatened fresh 50% duties on goods from cement to hockey sticks. Prime Minister Carney expected to speak with Trump directly.

Industry Impact

Cement's appearance on the target list matters for construction-linked chemicals: tariffs that raise building-material costs weigh on the construction demand that drives sealants, adhesives and coatings. The shift to Section 338 signals that US tariffs will persist even if courts curb the original legal basis, so manufacturers with cross-border North American supply chains should plan for durable duties rather than a quick reversal, and watch the 15% auto rate as a template for sector-by-sector relief.

USA Today | MarketScreener | BNN Bloomberg | The Globe and Mail | MarketScreener

item.title: The 60-day US–Iran ceasefire expired on 17 August with no new deal; Iran declared a "fully offensive" posture, Strait of Hormuz shipping fell about 90%, Trump threatened to bomb Oman, and Washington prepared unprecedented sanctions — sending oil higher.
item.description:
The truce that had paused the US–Iran war lapsed on 17 August. Tehran said it would shift to a "fully offensive" military stance, and the US ruled out extending the ceasefire. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — the channel carrying roughly one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil — dropped by around 90% as the US blockade of Iranian ports continued. President Trump raised the stakes by threatening to bomb Oman, the neutral Gulf state that had brokered shipping routes with Iran, if it interfered with the blockade. Separately, the US Treasury said it would unveil measures against Tehran "never seen before" as soon as next week, targeting oil traders, currency exchangers and banks — many based in China — that help Iran finance trade. Brent crude climbed and equity markets slipped as the risk of renewed supply disruption returned. This is a clear escalation from the fragile pause reported in recent alerts.

Industry Impact

For chemical and manufacturing buyers, the collapse of the truce revives the two channels that hurt most: higher and more volatile crude and naphtha prices (the feedstocks behind plastics, solvents and many adhesive raw materials), and disrupted Gulf shipping that lengthens lead times and lifts freight. Companies that ran down safety stock during the ceasefire face renewed pressure to rebuild buffers and re-check contract clauses tied to oil-linked surcharges.

Kompas.com | Süddeutsche Zeitung | The Nation | The Straits Times | Asharq Al-Awsat
